questiontext.text: In a game tree, what does the minimax value of a position represent?

answer.text: The best score MAX can guarantee assuming MIN plays optimally

feedback.text: Correct — minimax assumes an optimal opponent.

answer.text: The average score over all possible opponent moves

feedback.text: Minimax assumes optimal play, not an average.

answer.text: The score MAX gets if MIN plays randomly

feedback.text: Minimax assumes the opponent plays optimally, not randomly.

answer.text: The total number of leaf nodes

feedback.text: That is a size measure, not the minimax value.

generalfeedback.text: Minimax propagates values upward: MAX levels take the maximum child, MIN levels take the minimum, giving the score under optimal play by both sides.

questiontext.text: At a MIN node in the game tree, which value is chosen from the children?

feedback.text: Correct — MIN minimizes MAX's score.
That is what a MAX node does, not a MIN node.

answer.text: The average of the child values

feedback.text: MIN takes the minimum, not an average.
MIN plays optimally by choosing the minimum.

generalfeedback.text: Levels alternate: MAX nodes take the maximum child value and MIN nodes take the minimum, modeling both players playing optimally.

questiontext.text: Compared with plain minimax, what move does alpha-beta pruning return?

answer.text: Exactly the same move as plain minimax

feedback.text: Correct — alpha-beta only skips branches that cannot change the result.

answer.text: A better move than minimax could find

feedback.text: No — it returns the same optimal move, just faster.

answer.text: A slightly worse but faster move

feedback.text: Alpha-beta does not sacrifice quality; the move is identical.

answer.text: A random move among the top choices

feedback.text: It is exact, returning minimax's move.

generalfeedback.text: Alpha-beta prunes only branches that provably cannot affect the root decision, so it returns the identical move as minimax while examining fewer nodes.

questiontext.text: With ideal move ordering, roughly how many nodes does alpha-beta explore, for branching factor b and depth d?

feedback.text: Correct — effectively doubling the searchable depth.
That is plain minimax; good ordering cuts the exponent roughly in half.
The cost is exponential, not linear.
The exponent involves depth, roughly d/2, over base b.

generalfeedback.text: With good move ordering alpha-beta explores about O(b^(d/2)) nodes instead of O(b^d), effectively doubling the depth reachable for the same cost.

questiontext.text: Alpha-beta pruning can return a different (worse) move than plain minimax.

feedback.text: It prunes only branches that cannot affect the decision, so the move is identical.
Correct — alpha-beta returns exactly the same move as minimax.

questiontext.text: In alpha-beta pruning, α is the best value MAX can guarantee so far and β is the best value MIN can guarantee so far.

feedback.text: Correct — a branch is pruned once α ≥ β.
That is exactly what α and β track.

questiontext.text: What is the name of the algorithm that computes a position's value by alternating maximizing and minimizing levels? (one word)

feedback.text: Correct — minimax.
Correct — minimax.
Correct — minimax.

questiontext.text: Which statements about alpha-beta pruning are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It returns the same value as plain minimax

feedback.text: Yes — it is an exact optimization.

answer.text: Good move ordering improves how much it can prune

feedback.text: Yes — ordering strong moves first prunes more branches.

answer.text: It may miss the optimal move to run faster

feedback.text: No — it never prunes a branch that could change the decision.

answer.text: It always explores every leaf of the tree

feedback.text: No — its whole point is to skip provably irrelevant branches.

generalfeedback.text: Alpha-beta is exact (same value as minimax) and benefits from good move ordering, pruning branches that cannot affect the root — so it does not visit every leaf.
